Internal pitch deck ↗
Spark Studios · Dubai · Hassan Alnoon

Spark wants its own "Waldo": a place where its clients turn a vague idea into a brief Spark can price.

Spark Studios is a Dubai marketing agency that calls itself "the AI-native marketing company". Today its pre-sales is slow: long request forms, site visits and a chain of meetings that take about a month. Hassan wants a logged-in area on Spark's website. Clients add their brands, run a few guided AI chats (audience, brand and so on), and press Submit for proposal. Spark then sends back a professional proposal they can take to their boss.

The one thing to rememberThe chat itself is the easy part; Hassan said so. The design value is everything around it: organizing brands, picking the right workflow, seeing a summary build up, and an exit that turns the conversation into a boss-ready brief and a proposal request. Waldo has nothing like that last step.
Warm
Second project with this client. Eleken already did a design trial for Spark's client Cyber Factory.
Concept
Nothing built yet. Spark has an in-house dev team and vendor APIs.
Now
"Certainly. Immediately." Hassan's answer when asked about a start date.
Approvals
He needs the designs first to win internal approvals, then development.

Spark Studios and Hassan

Spark sells marketing strategy to C-level clients and brands itself as AI-first. The agent has to look like Spark, not like a Waldo reskin, because it sits on Spark's main website.

Company Fact

Spark Studios Advertising and Marketing L.L.C., Dubai (EULA names the courts of Dubai). One-page site at sparkstudios.ae, hero line "The AI-Native Marketing Company."

Five service disciplines: Brand Governance, Brand Strategy, Brand Innovation, Brand Marketing, Brand Performance. The site lists no case studies, client logos or team.

They describe an orchestration layer called "Spark OI (Operating Intelligence)" that "brings together the world's most creative humans with autonomous agents and tech to unlock growth as a service."

Hassan Alnoon Fact

Public profiles list him as Founder & CEO of Ghisha AI, a sovereign AI platform. He has about 15 years in tech and information security, an MSc in Information Security & Cryptography, and was in the UAE National Experts Program. "Ghisha" is also the first brand tile in his Waldo workspace in the call.

InferenceHe is a founder or owner at Spark: he approves the budget himself and owns the dev team ("It's my team"). Technical and security-minded, he'll ask about APIs and data.

Who uses it

The users are not Waldo's expert agency strategists. They're Spark's clients: people with an idea, no brief and a boss to convince.
"For Waldo, it's marketing agency, for us, but for me, it's gonna be my customer."Hassan, 29:21
Primary · the client lead

Marketing or brand lead at a UAE enterprise or government entity Inference

Based on Spark's services (governance, board-level reporting, mega events) and its live client, the UAE Cyber Factory (UAE Cyber Security Council and CPX).

  • Doesn't know what they want. "We just log in there, they don't know what they want" (30:57) Quote
  • Needs credibility upward. "they cannot just use a random chat GPT, they want to pull story, show the UI off." (31:50; "pull story" may be "full story") Quote
  • Juggles several ideas. "they can manage many ideas" (29:38) Quote
  • Can't write prompts well. The "articulation barrier": many users struggle to put intent into prompts (Nielsen) Fact
  • Wary of where data goes, likely for government accounts Inference
Secondary · Spark's team

Strategist or account lead receiving the submission Inference

They get the packaged conversation in "our backend" and write the proposal.

  • Needs structured, comparable input, not raw chat logs
  • Needs the client's stated preferences ("I like this colour, this direction")
  • Needs budget, timeline and decision-maker info to price
  • Wants fewer clarification meetings

Hassan didn't ask for this side to be designed. A light view of what Spark receives could still be a strong secondary (see Where to shoot).

UX patterns to borrow

Six patterns cover the whole product: URL-prefill onboarding, workflow cards with completion, guided questions in chat, a live summary next to the chat, a brand switcher in a sidebar, and a submit-for-review modal.

1 · Guided questions instead of a blank prompt

2 · A summary that builds next to the chat

3 · Workflow cards with done states

4 · Brand from a URL · 5 · Workspace switcher

6 · Submit to a human team

Images from Mobbin (© their apps). Links are in sources/research-competitors-patterns.md. Trust signals (sources panel, "reviewed by a strategist") are covered there too.

Proposed direction

A white, Spark-branded workspace: brands in a left sidebar, 4–6 workflow cards with progress, a chat with a summary panel that fills as you talk, and a submit that recaps everything before sending it to Spark.

Information architecture Inference

SidebarBrands → ideas/projects under each brand · + Add brand · Submitted proposals
Brand pageBrand card (AI-prefilled from the website) · workflow cards with status · progress "3 of 5" · Submit for proposal
WorkflowChat on the left, live summary on the right · "Mark done" / auto-done · Next workflow

A starting set of workflows Inference, to validate with Hassan

Hassan wants "something more sensible" than Waldo's list. A proposal mapped to Spark's five disciplines and to what Spark needs in order to quote:

#WorkflowOutput in summarySpark discipline
01Brand snapshotWho you are, from your website, confirmed by youGovernance / Strategy
02The ideaWhat you want to make or launch, and why nowInnovation
03AudienceWho it's for and what they care aboutStrategy
04CompetitorsWho else is there and where the gap isStrategy / Performance
05Look and feelDirections, colours, sample logos and moodboardInnovation / Marketing
06Goals, budget and timingSuccess metric, budget range, deadline, decision-makerNeeded to quote

Principles

  1. Never a blank page. Each workflow opens with the agent's first question and clickable options.
  2. The summary is the product. The chat is a means; the right panel is what the client keeps and what Spark receives.
  3. Visible progress. Cards go from not started to in progress to done (green), with "3 of 5" toward a strong proposal.
  4. Honest handoff. AI drafts, a Spark strategist writes the proposal, and the UI says so, with a reply time. It matches Spark's AI policy: estimates from the AI are "purely indicative and non-binding".
  5. Spark's look. White, black and dot-matrix, so it's clearly not Waldo.

Spark AI brief agent · Where to shoot

Win it at the exit: the moment a chat becomes a proposal request.

Hassan told us the chat is the easy part. The one thing he added on top of Waldo is Submit for proposal. It's where his cost saving happens, where his customer gets something to show their boss, and where Waldo has nothing.

The one pain point

"Not just ChatGPT": a brief credible enough to take upstairs

Design the living summary (it builds next to each chat) and the Submit for proposal moment (it recaps every summary, takes a comment, and promises a human reply) as the heart of the trial. Everything else serves those two screens.
"this is basic chat window, which is, okay, there's not much design here to be done, but what I want to add is… maybe a submit… submit for quotation."Hassan, 27:49
"a professional proposal with timelines and, you know, not just ChatGBT or something … for them to pitch to their management."Hassan, 31:50
"This is part of our roadmap. We need to do an AI agent capability to our customer to reduce the cost."Hassan, 30:57

Why this one

  • It's his addition. Everything else exists in Waldo; this is the "functionality on top" Maksym mentioned.
  • It's where the money is. It replaces the 100-page form and the month of meetings.
  • It's Waldo's real gap. In Hassan's own Waldo chat the agent offers "Print / Export This Chat" or "I Write It Here, You Copy It". There's no handoff to a team.
  • It serves both sides. The client gets a boss-ready brief; Spark gets structured input to price.

What the two hero screens must do

Living summary

  • Fills in as the client answers, section by section
  • Plain language; editable; "you said" vs "AI suggests" kept visibly separate
  • Becomes the card's output once done (green)

Submit for proposal

  • Recap: which workflows are done, with a nudge if key ones (budget, timing) are missing
  • Optional comment ("I like direction B")
  • What happens next: a Spark strategist, reply time, an indicative-only note
  • Afterwards: a status card (Submitted → In review → Proposal ready)
Secondary targets

Five that make the hero land

  1. Brands and ideas in a sidebar. "it needs to be organized a bit better, maybe on the side" (31:50). Persistent navigation, several ideas per brand.
  2. A sensible workflow set. "Maybe not these, you will select something else, something more sensible." Four to six cards in a suggested order, with done states and "3 of 5".
  3. Spark's own look. White, black, dot-matrix type, the "Spark Operating Intelligence" voice. It must read as Spark's product on Spark's site, not a Waldo reskin.
  4. Never a blank chat. The agent opens each workflow with a question and options, because users "don't know what they want".
  5. Add a brand from a website (stretch). Spark's current chat already starts with "share your website", and Waldo pre-fills category and logo.
Stretch with high upside: a single "what Spark receives" view, the submission as a strategist sees it. It shows Hassan where his cost saving happens, which helps his internal approvals.
Don't spend time on

Low return for the trial

  • Credits, plans, pricing, the API layer: Waldo complexity Hassan wants to avoid ("very minimal")
  • Polishing chat bubbles: he said there's "not much design here"
  • Marketing pages or the hero animation on sparkstudios.ae
  • Report export, publish or scheduling

The playback, in one sentence

"Your client logs in on sparkstudios.ae, adds a brand, works through a few guided chats that each leave a clear summary, then presses Submit for proposal, and your team sends back a professional proposal they can take to their boss. Right?"
Questions

Must ask

  1. Who approves this internally, and when? ("I need this for some other approvals.") What format convinces them: prototype, deck, video?
  2. Which "vendor APIs"? Waldo's (Build), Spark's own onboarding/chat, or both? Can we see a sample response: text only, or also sources, images, structured sections?
  3. Which workflows? Show our set of six (brand snapshot, the idea, audience, competitors, look and feel, goals/budget/timing). Keep, cut or add?
  4. What does Spark need to write a proposal? Budget range, deadline, decision-maker, scope? This becomes the required "readiness" before Submit.
  5. Who are the users? Enterprise and government marketing leads, or startups and founders too? English only, or Arabic / RTL?

Good to ask

  1. Does this replace the current "Spark Operating Intelligence" chat on the homepage, or sit behind it?
  2. After Submit: how does the client get the proposal (in the app, email, a call)? What reply time can Spark promise?
  3. Should the agent generate visuals (sample logos, moodboards) like in Waldo?
  4. Is it free for clients? Any limits?
  5. Should a client's colleagues be able to join a brand?
  6. Desktop only for now?
  7. What would make you say the trial was a success?
Likely pushback

Objections and answers

He saysWe say
"It's just a chat, there's not much to design."Agreed. That's why we focus on what's around it: how brands are organized, which workflow to start, the summary they keep, and the submit that saves you the meetings.
"Why not just use Waldo? We're partners."Waldo ends in a report for agency strategists. Yours ends in a Spark proposal for your own clients, on your site, in your brand.
"Just tell me the cost."One designer, one number per phase: free trial, then an MVP of about X weeks at Y. Agree internally before the call.
"Development may not start soon."Fine. The trial is built for your approvals. We hand over to your team when you're ready.
"Our data is sensitive."We design what the client sees: disclosure, an "AI drafts, Spark reviews" line, privacy cues. Your AI policy already sets the tone.
Close

The ask at the end

  • Trial start date and Day-5 presentation slot
  • An intro to the dev lead ("It's my team, I'll connect you with them")
  • Names of the internal approvers, and an invite to the final presentation if possible
  • Agreement that a contract follows a successful trial, with both projects on separate budgets

Background: dossier · where to shoot · trial scope

Spark AI brief agent · Research summary

The summary, without the filler.

Client

Spark Studios, Dubai: "The AI-Native Marketing Company". Hassan Alnoon (also CEO of Ghisha AI, security background) owns the budget and the dev team. A warm account: Eleken already designed a trial for their client Cyber Factory.

Problem

Pre-sales is slow and expensive (100-page forms, site visits, about a month of meetings). Their customers come with ideas but no brief, and need something credible to get budget.

Product

Behind a login on sparkstudios.ae: add brands → 4–6 workflow cards → one guided chat per workflow with a summary → green when done → Submit for proposal + comment → Spark returns a professional proposal.

Concept only. Vendor APIs exist and the in-house dev team will build it. Designs are needed first for internal approvals. "Very minimal", "our own interface", "not their flow".

Users

Spark's own clients, not agency strategists. Likely enterprise and government marketing leads who "don't know what they want" and must pitch upward.

Reference: Waldo

Brands → tabs → 12–50+ generic workflows that run as one-shot reports, plus a strategy chat. Dark teal and magenta. Credits and plans. It has no handoff to a human team.

Keep: brand-first structure, URL prefill, "launch next workflow", visible research steps. Change: sidebar navigation, fewer and client-facing workflows, chat plus summary instead of form plus report. Drop: credits, export, scheduling.

Market

Brand-intelligence tools serve experts and stop at insight. Intake tools (ReqBrief) stop at a brief. None we found ends in a studio's human proposal, so that's Spark's angle. (Hypothesis from targeted searches.)

Patterns

Guided question cardsLive summary panelCards with done statesBrand from URLSidebar switcherSubmit for review modal

Where to shoot

The living summary and the Submit for proposal moment. Secondaries: sidebar organization, a sensible workflow set, Spark's own look, never a blank chat.

Trial

5 screens in Spark's style, as a prototype, plus a one-page vision and timeline. Exactly what Hassan asked for.
